---
title: "Indirect Comparison and Bucher's Theorem"
---

## Introduction {#sec-bucher-intro}

A health technology assessment routinely faces a question that the available trials never asked. A
regulator must decide whether a new drug $A$ is better than an established drug $B$, but the two have
never been compared head to head. To keep a concrete picture in view throughout the chapter, let $A$ be a
*new* statin and $B$ an *established* statin, each tested in its own randomized trial against the *same*
comparator $C$ (a placebo or standard of care), with an unfavorable cardiovascular event as the outcome.
What does exist is a trial of $A$ against $C$, and a separate trial of $B$ against the same comparator
$C$. The clinical question is about $A$ versus $B$; the evidence speaks only about $A$ versus $C$ and $B$
versus $C$. The task of this chapter is to make precise the simplest device that bridges the gap: the
**anchored indirect comparison**, and the theorem of @bucher1997 that governs it.

The idea is disarmingly simple. If the effect of $A$ relative to $C$ is $d_{AC}$ and the effect of $B$
relative to $C$ is $d_{BC}$, both measured on a scale where contrasts add, then the effect of $A$
relative to $B$ ought to be the difference $d_{AC}-d_{BC}$, because the common comparator $C$ cancels.
Replacing the unknown true effects by their trial estimates gives the **Bucher estimator**
$\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$. The algebra is the algebra of a triangle. What makes the chapter a
piece of mathematics rather than a piece of arithmetic is the question of *when the algebra is licensed*.
The estimator is unbiased only if the true effect of $A$ versus $C$ is the same quantity in the $A$
versus $C$ trial as it would be in the (hypothetical) population where we want to report $A$ versus $B$,
and likewise for $B$ versus $C$. That requirement is the **transitivity** assumption, equivalently the
**constancy of relative effects**. It is the load-bearing hypothesis of every method in this book, and
the rest of the book is, in a precise sense, the study of what to do when it fails.

We prove four things in full. First, that the relative effects on a fixed scale obey an antisymmetry law
and an additivity law within any single population, so that $d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}$ is a tautology *inside
one population* (@lem-relative-effect-algebra). Second, that under transitivity the same identity holds
*across* the three trial populations, which is the content of constancy (@prp-transitivity-consistency).
Third, that the Bucher estimator is then unbiased for the cross-population contrast (@thm-bucher-unbiased),
with variance equal to the sum of the two direct variances under independence (@thm-bucher-variance).
Fourth, that the common comparator is exactly what cancels the study-specific baselines, so that the
anchored comparison is protected against a bias that destroys the naive single-arm comparison
(@prp-baseline-cancellation, @prp-unanchored-bias). A fully worked example on the log odds-ratio scale,
computed from raw two-by-two tables, closes the development.

Throughout we use the relative-effect notation of [Notation](/notation.qmd): $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ is the
marginal effect of treatment $b$ versus treatment $a$ in population $\mathcal P$, on a stated scale, and
$\hat d_{ab(j)}$ is its estimator from study $j$. The potential-outcome machinery of Chapter 9
(@def-potential-outcome, @def-ate, @thm-ate-identification) supplies the meaning of a single trial's
relative effect; the inference tools of Chapter 5 (@thm-delta-method, @thm-mle-asymptotic-normality)
supply its standard error. This chapter corresponds to results D.1 to D.4 of the proof catalogue.

## A running example and a map of the argument {#sec-bucher-running}

Before any formalism, fix the picture we will return to at every turn. Two randomized trials share the
comparator $C$ (placebo):

- Trial $AC$ compares the new statin $A$ with placebo $C$ and reports an odds ratio of the cardiovascular
  event of $2$ for $C$ versus $A$; on the log scale, $\hat d_{AC}=\log 2\approx 0.69$. In words, placebo
  patients had twice the odds of the event, so $A$ is protective.
- Trial $BC$ compares the established statin $B$ with placebo $C$ and reports an odds ratio of $1.5$ for
  $C$ versus $B$; on the log scale, $\hat d_{BC}=\log 1.5\approx 0.41$. Placebo patients had one and a
  half times the odds, so $B$ is protective too, but less so.

We will compute the full example from raw counts in @sec-bucher-example; the two trials there produce
exactly these numbers.

**What "population" means here.** By a *population* we do not mean the specific people enrolled, but the
*distribution* of their baseline characteristics: the mix of ages, disease severities, and risk factors a
trial would draw from. Formally it is a probability distribution over the covariate space $\mathcal X$.
The two trials draw from two different such distributions, $\mathcal P_{AC}$ and $\mathcal P_{BC}$, and we
will also speak of a third, $\mathcal P_{AB}$: the population in which we actually want the $A$-versus-$B$
answer, typically the patients who would receive the drug in routine care. No trial was ever run in
$\mathcal P_{AB}$ for $A$ against $B$; that absence is the entire reason an indirect comparison is needed.

**Two recurring words.** A **contrast** is a difference of two positions on the chosen scale, such as
$\eta_B-\eta_A$; it is the mathematical form of the phrase "relative effect." The **link scale** is the
transformed scale (log-odds for a probability, log for a rate or hazard, or the untransformed mean for a
continuous outcome) on which we agree to do all subtraction, chosen precisely so that contrasts add along
a path.

The available and missing comparisons form a triangle:

```
              A  - - - - - - - - -  B        target contrast d_AB
               \                   /            (dashed: NO A-vs-B trial)
                \                 /
          d_AC   \               /   d_BC
       (trial AC) \             / (trial BC)
                   \           /
                    \         /
                     \       /
                        C                     common comparator (the anchor)
```

The two solid legs $A\!-\!C$ and $B\!-\!C$ are the trials we have; the dashed edge $A\!-\!B$ is the
comparison we want. Bucher walks the triangle: go from $A$ down to $C$, then from $C$ up to $B$, and the
detour through $C$ recovers the missing edge.

::: {.remark}
**The object, stated once, up front.** Everything below serves one formula. Writing $\hat d_{AC}$ and
$\hat d_{BC}$ for the two trials' estimated log-scale effects against the shared comparator $C$, the
**Bucher estimator** of the $A$-versus-$B$ effect is the single subtraction
$$
\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC},
$$
with standard error $\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}$ when the two trials are independent. In
the running example $\hat d_{AC}=\log 2$ and $\hat d_{BC}=\log 1.5$, so
$\hat d_{AB}=\log 2-\log 1.5=\log\tfrac43\approx 0.29$: the indirect odds ratio of the event for $B$
versus $A$ is $\tfrac43$. The rest of the chapter answers one question: *when is this subtraction
allowed?* $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

**Orientation, once and for all.** The single most common source of confusion in indirect comparison is
sign. We follow [Notation](/notation.qmd): $d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a$ places the *reference* treatment first
and the *active* treatment second. Because the outcome is unfavorable, a *positive* contrast flags
*higher, hence worse,* odds for the treatment in the second slot. The following table translates between
the applied phrasing and this chapter's symbols; keep it at hand.

| Applied phrasing | This chapter's symbol | Equals | A positive value means |
|---|---|---|---|
| effect of $C$ relative to $A$ | $d_{AC}$ | $\eta_C-\eta_A$ | $C$ has higher (worse) event odds than $A$, so $A$ is protective |
| "$A$ versus $C$" (common applied phrasing) | $-d_{AC}$ | $\eta_A-\eta_C$ | $A$ has higher (worse) event odds than $C$ |
| effect of $B$ relative to $A$ (the **target**) | $d_{AB}$ | $\eta_B-\eta_A$ | $B$ has higher (worse) event odds than $A$, so $A$ is the better statin |
| the Bucher combination | $d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$ | $(\eta_C-\eta_A)-(\eta_C-\eta_B)$ | the shared $\eta_C$ cancels |

In the running example $\hat d_{AC}=\log 2>0$ says placebo is worse than $A$; $\hat d_{AB}=\log\tfrac43>0$
says $B$ has slightly higher event odds than $A$, so on this evidence $A$ is the better statin.

**Map of the argument.** The chapter has one destination (the subtraction is licensed and its variance
is known) reached through five results. This table is a scaffold; each entry is proved below.

| Result | Plain statement | Its job in the indirect comparison |
|---|---|---|
| @lem-relative-effect-algebra | contrasts reverse sign and add along a path | makes $d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}$ arithmetic *inside one population* |
| @def-transitivity, @prp-transitivity-consistency | the relevant effects are the same in every trial population | lets that subtraction carry *across* the three populations |
| @thm-bucher-unbiased | the Bucher estimator has the right expectation | the indirect estimate is on target |
| @thm-bucher-variance | its variance is the sum of the two direct variances | indirect evidence is less precise than direct |
| @prp-baseline-cancellation, @prp-unanchored-bias | the anchor cancels the study baselines | anchored comparison beats the naive single-arm one |

## The relative effect and its scale {#sec-bucher-scale}

The goal of this section is modest but easy to lose sight of: we want to put every treatment arm on a
single additive scale, a number $\eta_k$ we can subtract, so that "effect" becomes "difference."
Everything in the section is machinery for doing that honestly when the outcome is binary or a survival
time rather than a plain average.

Fix three treatments $A$, $B$, $C$ and a strictly increasing, differentiable **link function** $g$
(@def-link-function) that maps a mean outcome to a "linear-predictor" scale on which effects are to be
reported: the logit for binary outcomes (giving log odds ratios), the log for rates and hazards (giving
log rate or hazard ratios), and the identity for continuous outcomes (giving mean differences). For a
treatment $k\in\{A,B,C\}$ write $\mu_k(x)=\mathbb E[Y(k)\mid X=x]$ for the conditional mean of the
potential outcome under $k$ (@def-potential-outcome), as a function of the baseline covariates
$x\in\mathcal X$.

::: {#def-marginal-link-position}
## Marginal link-scale position
Let $\mathcal P$ be a population with covariate density $f_{\mathcal P}$. The **marginal mean** of
treatment $k$ in $\mathcal P$ is $\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}=\int \mu_k(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx$, and its
**marginal link-scale position** is
$$
\eta_{k(\mathcal P)} \;=\; g\!\left(\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}\right)
\;=\; g\!\left(\int \mu_k(x)\,f_{\mathcal P}(x)\,dx\right).
$$ {#eq-bucher-eta}
The **marginal relative effect** of treatment $b$ versus treatment $a$ in $\mathcal P$ (@def-marginal-effect)
is the contrast of link-scale positions,
$$
d_{ab(\mathcal P)} \;=\; \eta_{b(\mathcal P)}-\eta_{a(\mathcal P)}
\;=\; g\!\left(\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P)}\right)-g\!\left(\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P)}\right).
$$ {#eq-bucher-reldef}
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The phrase "link-scale position" is jargon coined here; take it to mean "the
arm's adjusted location on the report scale, before we subtract two arms." The object $\eta_{k(\mathcal P)}$
is a two-step recipe. Step one: in population $\mathcal P$, work out the *average* outcome you would see
if everyone took treatment $k$; this is the inner integral $\bar\mu_{k(\mathcal P)}$, an ordinary
population mean. Step two: push that single average through the link $g$ to land on the additive scale
(the logit of a probability, the log of a rate). The relative effect $d_{ab(\mathcal P)}$ is then just the
gap between two such numbers. One notational caution: $\eta_{k(\mathcal P)}$ is a *population-level*
(marginal) quantity indexed by a treatment and a population; it is **not** the individual-level linear
predictor $\eta_{ijk}$ of [Notation](/notation.qmd), which carries a person, study, and arm subscript.
Same Greek letter, a coarser object. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Two further points of interpretation deserve emphasis before we use @eq-bucher-reldef.

::: {.remark}
**Marginal, not conditional.** Equation @eq-bucher-reldef marginalizes the conditional means *first*
(the inner integral) and applies the link *second*. This is the effect a trial reports when it compares
arm-level summaries: the marginal odds ratio, the marginal hazard ratio. It is in general not equal to
the conditional effect $g(\mu_b(x))-g(\mu_a(x))$ averaged over $x$, because a nonlinear $g$ does not
commute with averaging. Here is the phenomenon in one line of arithmetic: if half a population has event
probability $0.9$ and half has $0.1$, the average probability is $0.5$ with logit $0$, whereas the
average of the two logits is $\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}(0.9)+\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}(0.1)=0$ only
by the symmetry of this toy case; shift the split to $0.8$ and $0.1$ and $g$ of the average
($\operatorname{logit}0.45=-0.20$) no longer equals the average of the $g$'s
($\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}0.8+\tfrac12\operatorname{logit}0.1\approx-0.40$). For the identity link the
two always coincide; for the logit and log links they differ, the phenomenon of non-collapsibility
(@def-non-collapsibility, @def-collapsibility, @thm-noncollapsibility-or-hr). The Bucher construction
operates on whatever marginal effects the trials report, and the transitivity assumption below is a
statement about those marginal effects. We return to the interaction between non-collapsibility and
indirect comparison in Chapter 16. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why a scale on which contrasts add.** The whole construction lives on the link scale precisely because
on that scale a relative effect is a *difference* of two positions, and differences subtract cleanly. On
the natural outcome scale the same information is multiplicative: an odds ratio of $A$ versus $C$ times
the odds ratio of $C$ versus $B$ gives the odds ratio of $A$ versus $B$. Taking logarithms turns the
product into the sum @eq-bucher-reldef. The risk difference is the one common effect measure that adds
on the identity scale directly. We make the additive structure a lemma in @sec-bucher-algebra. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

### The single trial as a source of an unbiased contrast {#sec-bucher-singletrial}

A randomized trial comparing two of the treatments in a population $\mathcal P$ delivers an (approximately)
unbiased estimator of the corresponding marginal relative effect @eq-bucher-reldef. We record this as the
input to everything that follows; the proof is the identification argument of Chapter 9. The reader who
wants only the upshot may read the proposition, skip its proof, and note the plain-language remark that
follows it.

::: {#prp-trial-unbiased}
## A randomized trial estimates its own marginal contrast
Let study $j$ randomize patients drawn from population $\mathcal P_j$ between arms $a$ and $b$, with
randomization probability $P(T=b\mid X=x)=\pi\in(0,1)$ independent of $x$. Then the arms satisfy
ignorability and positivity (@def-ignorability, @def-positivity) by design, the arm means identify the
marginal potential-outcome means $\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)}$ and $\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P_j)}$
(@thm-ate-identification), and any estimator $\hat d_{ab(j)}$ formed by applying $g$ to consistent arm-mean
estimators is consistent for $d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}$, with $\mathbb E[\hat d_{ab(j)}]\to d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Randomization makes the treatment indicator $T$ independent of the potential outcomes $(Y(a),Y(b))$ and
of the covariates $X$; in particular $T\perp (Y(a),Y(b))\mid X$ holds with the conditioning on $X$
vacuous, which is ignorability (@def-ignorability), and $\pi\in(0,1)$ is positivity (@def-positivity). By
the identification theorem (@thm-ate-identification) applied within $\mathcal P_j$, the observed mean in
arm $a$, namely $\mathbb E[Y\mid T=a]$, equals $\mathbb E[Y(a)]=\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)}$, and likewise for
$b$. An estimator that plugs consistent arm-mean estimators $\widehat{\bar\mu}_{a(j)},\widehat{\bar\mu}_{b(j)}$
into $g$ and differences them is, by the continuous mapping theorem and the differentiability of $g$,
consistent for $g(\bar\mu_{b(\mathcal P_j)})-g(\bar\mu_{a(\mathcal P_j)})=d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}$; its bias
vanishes in the limit, and to first order in the delta-method expansion of @sec-bucher-logodds it is
unbiased. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the proof said, in plain words.** *Ignorability* means that, thanks to randomization, which
treatment a patient received tells you nothing about how they would have fared under either treatment; the
two arms are exchangeable. Because the coin flip is independent of everything about the patient, the
conditioning on $X$ is "vacuous," that is, unnecessary. *Positivity* is just $\pi\in(0,1)$: everyone had a
genuine chance of either arm. Together these are what a randomized trial buys you by design, so the arm
averages estimate the population averages you would have seen if everyone had taken that treatment.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Consistent, and unbiased to first order.** A subtlety worth stating plainly: the empirical log
odds-ratio is *not exactly* unbiased in a finite sample. What @prp-trial-unbiased delivers is (i)
*consistency*, meaning that as the arm sizes grow, $\hat d_{ab(j)}$ converges in probability to the true
contrast, and (ii) *first-order (asymptotic) unbiasedness*, meaning the leading term of its bias vanishes
as the sample grows. Every use of the word "unbiased" in this chapter, including in the statement of
Bucher's theorem below, is meant in this large-sample sense, which is the scale on which all Bucher
calculations operate. For trials of realistic size the distinction is harmless; we flag it only so the
word is not over-read. A separate warning about the word *consistent*: in @prp-trial-unbiased it is the
statistical sense (an estimator converging to its target); in @eq-bucher-consistency below it is the
network-meta-analysis sense (direct and indirect estimates *agreeing*). The two senses are unrelated;
context disambiguates. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The phrase "unbiased estimator of $d_{AC}$" in Bucher's theorem is shorthand for the conclusion of
@prp-trial-unbiased: each trial estimates *its own* population's marginal contrast without (first-order)
bias. The entire subtlety of indirect comparison is that the trial estimates the contrast in *its*
population $\mathcal P_j$, whereas we wish to combine the trials into a statement about a single contrast.
Bridging the populations is the work of the transitivity assumption.

## The algebra of contrasts {#sec-bucher-algebra}

Inside a single population the relative effects @eq-bucher-reldef are differences of three numbers
$\eta_{A},\eta_{B},\eta_{C}$ (suppressing the population subscript), and therefore satisfy two
elementary laws. They are the entire algebraic content of Bucher's identity; the statistics enters only
through @prp-trial-unbiased and the variance bookkeeping of @sec-bucher-variance.

It is fair to ask why a book states a theorem for something so elementary. The reason is that this
trivial algebra is the *entire* mathematical skeleton of the Bucher estimator: the variance result
(@thm-bucher-variance), the cancellation of baselines (@prp-baseline-cancellation), and the unbiasedness
theorem (@thm-bucher-unbiased) all reduce to the two laws below applied on the right scale. Naming them
now lets those later proofs cite them by name rather than re-derive them.

::: {#lem-relative-effect-algebra}
## Antisymmetry and additivity of contrasts
Fix a population $\mathcal P$ and let $d_{ab}=\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}$ for $a,b\in\{A,B,C\}$ as in
@eq-bucher-reldef. Then for all treatments $a,b,c$:

1. **Antisymmetry (reversal):** $d_{ab}=-d_{ba}$, and in particular $d_{aa}=0$.

2. **Additivity (the triangle identity):**
$$
d_{ac} \;=\; d_{ab}+d_{bc}, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-additivity}
:::

::: {.proof}
Both laws are immediate from the representation $d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a$. For antisymmetry,
$d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a=-(\eta_a-\eta_b)=-d_{ba}$, and setting $b=a$ gives $d_{aa}=\eta_a-\eta_a=0$. For
additivity,
$$
d_{ab}+d_{bc}=(\eta_b-\eta_a)+(\eta_c-\eta_b)=\eta_c-\eta_a=d_{ac}.
$$
Adding $-d_{bc}$ to both sides of $d_{ac}=d_{ab}+d_{bc}$ and using antisymmetry rearranges this to
$d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}$. The middle term $\eta_b$ cancels because it enters $d_{ab}$ with a plus sign and
$d_{bc}$ with a minus sign; this cancellation of the intermediate treatment's link-scale position is the
algebraic seed of the indirect comparison. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** Read the triangle identity with the roles of the running example: setting
$a=A,b=C,c=B$ in $d_{ab}=d_{ac}-d_{bc}$ gives exactly $d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$, the Bucher combination. The
lemma says this is a *tautology* whenever all three contrasts live in one population; the whole difficulty,
taken up next, is that our three contrasts come from three different populations. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**A note on index order and the clinical convention.** With the convention of [Notation](/notation.qmd),
$d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a$ places the *reference* treatment first and the *active* treatment second. The
common comparator of an anchored comparison is $C$, so the two trial contrasts that involve $C$ are
$d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A$ and $d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B$, in which $C$ occupies the second slot; the target
contrast between the two new treatments is $d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A$. Much applied writing uses the opposite
order, "$A$ versus $C$," and reports $-d_{AC}=\eta_A-\eta_C$. By the antisymmetry law
@lem-relative-effect-algebra(1) the two orderings differ only by an overall sign and carry identical
information; the indirect identity $d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$ holds verbatim in either bookkeeping, because
reversing all three contrasts negates both sides. The practical rule to remember, tabulated in
@sec-bucher-running: with an *unfavorable* outcome, a **positive** $d_{ab}$ means the second-slot
treatment has the higher (worse) odds. We keep the [Notation](/notation.qmd) order and let the reader
translate by the reversal law where a "$A$ versus $C$" phrasing is more natural. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The additivity law @eq-bucher-additivity is a tautology when all three contrasts live in *one*
population, where the $\eta$'s are three fixed numbers. The trials, however, live in three different
populations $\mathcal P_{AB}$, $\mathcal P_{AC}$, $\mathcal P_{BC}$, each with its own $\eta$'s. To carry
@eq-bucher-additivity across populations we need exactly the assumption that the relevant contrasts do
not depend on which population we evaluate them in.

## Constancy of relative effects and transitivity {#sec-bucher-transitivity}

Before the formal definitions, the assumption in plain terms, because it is the most important idea in
the chapter. The two trials were run in different populations. Anchoring (Section
@sec-bucher-cancellation) will handle any difference in *baseline risk* for free. What it cannot handle is
a difference in the *size of a treatment effect* between the populations. A covariate that changes the
size of a treatment effect is an **effect modifier** (@def-effect-modifier); a covariate that shifts
outcomes but leaves treatment effects unchanged is a **prognostic variable** (@def-prognostic-variable).
Transitivity is the assumption that the trial populations are alike in their effect modifiers, and it
allows them to differ freely in everything else.

| Question about the trial populations | Answer under transitivity |
|---|---|
| What **must** be similar? | The distribution of any *effect modifier* of the relevant relative effects, that is, any covariate that changes the size of a treatment effect. |
| What is **allowed** to differ? | Baseline risk and purely *prognostic* factors, which shift outcomes but not treatment effects; the anchor cancels these (@prp-baseline-cancellation). |
| What **cannot** be repaired by more data? | Bias from an imbalance in effect modifiers. It is a bias, not a variance, so a larger trial does not shrink it. |

::: {.remark}
**A clinical instance, before the algebra.** Return to the two statin trials. Suppose age modifies the
effect of statin $B$ versus placebo $C$: the reduction in cardiovascular events is larger in older
patients. If the $BC$ trial enrolled a substantially younger population than the one in which we want to
report $A$ versus $B$, then $\hat d_{BC}$ estimates $B$'s effect in a *younger* population, and
subtracting it from $\hat d_{AC}$ silently mixes two different populations; transitivity fails. If instead
age only *predicts* cardiovascular risk but does *not* change the size of the statin effect, then age is a
prognostic variable, not an effect modifier: it shifts a study's baseline but not its treatment effect,
and anchoring absorbs the difference at no cost. Transitivity is thus a statement about effect modifiers,
not about baseline comparability. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#def-constancy-relative-effects}
## Constancy of relative effects
Let a network of studies be given, study $j$ having population $\mathcal P_j$ with covariate density
$f_j$. The marginal relative effect of $b$ versus $a$ in $\mathcal P_j$ on the scale $g$ is, as in
@eq-bucher-reldef,
$$
d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}=g\!\left(\int \mu_b(x)\,f_j(x)\,dx\right)-g\!\left(\int \mu_a(x)\,f_j(x)\,dx\right).
$$
The **constancy of relative effects** assumption asserts that this quantity does not depend on the
population: for every ordered pair of treatments $(a,b)$ and all studies $j,j'$,
$$
d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)} \;=\; d_{ab(\mathcal P_{j'})} \;=:\; d_{ab}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-constancy}
The common value $d_{ab}$ is then a population-free **network contrast**. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Constancy says every relative effect in the network is a single number that does
not care which study you look at, so "the effect of $b$ versus $a$" is well defined without naming a
population. It is the general network assumption. Transitivity, defined next, is its restriction to the
one triangle $\{A,B,C\}$ we need for a single Bucher comparison: constancy for the whole network,
transitivity for the triangle. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Constancy @eq-bucher-constancy is a property of every pair of treatments across every study. For a single
indirect comparison we need only its restriction to the triangle $\{A,B,C\}$ and the three populations in
play. That restriction is the transitivity assumption.

::: {#def-transitivity}
## Transitivity (for the anchored triangle)
Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be three treatments studied in populations $\mathcal P_{AB}$, $\mathcal P_{AC}$,
$\mathcal P_{BC}$ (the population of a hypothetical direct $A$-versus-$B$ trial, and the populations of
the available $A$-versus-$C$ and $B$-versus-$C$ trials). The **transitivity** assumption asserts that each
of the three relative effects takes the same value in every one of the three populations:
$$
d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AB(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{AB},
$$ {#eq-bucher-transitivity}
and likewise $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{AC}$ and
$d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=:d_{BC}$. Equivalently, transitivity
is the restriction of constancy @eq-bucher-constancy to the treatment triangle $\{A,B,C\}$. $\blacktriangleleft$

[machine-checked: `theories/Bucher.v`, `Definition transitivity`]
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** Transitivity says: the number you would call "the effect of $B$ versus $C$" is the
*same* number whether you measure it in the $A$-vs-$C$ trial's population, the $B$-vs-$C$ trial's
population, or the target population where you actually want the answer, and likewise for the other two
contrasts. It does *not* require the populations to be alike in every way; it requires them to be alike in
the ingredients that change treatment effects, the effect modifiers. It is the population-level cousin of
"no unmeasured confounding": ignorability (@def-ignorability) lets one study impersonate a randomized
experiment, and transitivity lets three studies impersonate one connected experiment run in a single
population. In practice a reviewer checks it not from the data but from the trial reports, by asking
whether the trials enrolled comparable patients with respect to known effect modifiers of the outcome; it
is a judgment about clinical similarity, informed by subject-matter knowledge, that the data alone cannot
confirm. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The next proposition makes the bridge precise: under transitivity the additivity law @eq-bucher-additivity,
a tautology inside one population, becomes a genuine relation among the three well-defined network
contrasts.

::: {#prp-transitivity-consistency}
## Transitivity yields the population consistency equation
Under transitivity (@def-transitivity), the network contrasts satisfy the **consistency equation**
$$
d_{AB} \;=\; d_{AC}-d_{BC}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-consistency}
Conversely, if the relative effects in each population obey the within-population additivity law
@eq-bucher-additivity and the consistency equation @eq-bucher-consistency holds for the common values,
then the three contrasts are mutually consistent in the sense required by @def-transitivity.

[machine-checked: `theories/Bucher.v`, `Lemma transitivity_subtract`, `Lemma subtract_transitivity`]
:::

::: {.proof}
By @def-transitivity the three symbols $d_{AB},d_{AC},d_{BC}$ are well defined, each being the common
value of a relative effect across the three populations. Evaluate the within-population additivity law
@lem-relative-effect-algebra(2) in, say, the population $\mathcal P_{AC}$:
$$
d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}.
$$
Transitivity replaces each population-specific effect on the right and the left by its common value,
$d_{AB(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AB}$, $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC}$, $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{BC}$, giving
$d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$, which is @eq-bucher-consistency. The same conclusion follows from evaluating the
additivity law in any of the three populations, since transitivity forces them to agree.

For the converse, suppose each population obeys @eq-bucher-additivity and the common values obey
@eq-bucher-consistency. Then in any population $\mathcal P_j$ the additivity law reads
$d_{AB(\mathcal P_j)}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_j)}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_j)}$; if two of the three contrasts are constant
across populations the third is forced to equal $d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}$, the common value, in every
population, which is @def-transitivity. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reading the two directions.** The forward direction is the one an analyst uses; the table records both.

| Direction | Assume | Conclude | Who uses it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forward | transitivity (@def-transitivity) | consistency equation @eq-bucher-consistency | @thm-bucher-unbiased, the whole method |
| Converse | within-population additivity plus consistency of the common values | transitivity | bookkeeping only |

The converse is a consistency check, not something a data analyst invokes: it says the three contrasts
cannot be *defined* inconsistently. "If two of the three are constant across populations, the third is
forced" because inside each population the three already satisfy $d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$ by pure algebra
(@lem-relative-effect-algebra), so fixing any two of them across populations pins the third by
subtraction. Which two does not matter; the algebra is symmetric. A first-time reader can take the forward
direction and move on. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
The Coq development encodes transitivity in the equivalent additive form $d_{AC}=d_{AB}+d_{BC}$
(`Definition transitivity`) and proves the two implications $d_{AC}=d_{AB}+d_{BC}\Rightarrow d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}$
(`Lemma transitivity_subtract`) and its converse (`Lemma subtract_transitivity`); these are precisely the
two directions of @prp-transitivity-consistency, stripped to their field algebra. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The anchored indirect comparison {#sec-bucher-anchored}

We can now name the estimator and the contrasting naive alternative it improves upon.

::: {#def-anchored-comparison}
## Anchored indirect comparison
Suppose study $AC$ provides an estimator $\hat d_{AC}$ of the $A$-versus-$C$ network contrast and study
$BC$ provides an estimator $\hat d_{BC}$ of the $B$-versus-$C$ network contrast, the two studies sharing
the common comparator $C$. The **anchored indirect comparison** of $A$ and $B$, or **Bucher estimator**,
is
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}} \;:=\; \hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-estimator}
The comparison is called *anchored* because the within-study contrasts to the shared comparator $C$ (the
anchor) are differenced, rather than the bare arm-level outcomes. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation and orientation.** The estimator subtracts the two "versus $C$" log-effects. In the
chapter's orientation the result estimates $d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A$, so a **positive** Bucher estimate means
$B$ has the higher (with an unfavorable outcome, worse) odds, hence $A$ is the better treatment. In the
running example $\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\log 2-\log 1.5=\log\tfrac43>0$: $B$ carries slightly
higher event odds than $A$. Always restate the direction when reporting: "$B$ versus $A$, higher is worse."
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

We also name the *wrong* thing to do, because seeing why it is wrong is the fastest route to seeing why
anchoring works. The following naive comparison is a foil: it is what you get if you ignore the common
comparator and simply compare the two active arms across studies. It is used in practice only as a last
resort, for disconnected networks (Chapter 26); here it is the cautionary contrast that makes the value of
the anchor visible.

::: {#def-unanchored-comparison}
## Unanchored (naive single-arm) comparison
With the same two studies, the **unanchored comparison** discards the comparator arms and contrasts the
two *active* arms directly across studies:
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{naive}} \;:=\; \hat\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\hat\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})},
$$ {#eq-bucher-naive}
where $\hat\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}$ is the estimated link-scale outcome of arm $A$ in study $AC$, and
$\hat\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ that of arm $B$ in study $BC$. This comparison ignores the anchor $C$
entirely. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation.** The unanchored estimator throws away the placebo arms and directly compares the
new statin's event rate in one trial to the established statin's event rate in the other. That is exactly
what you would do if you had two single-arm studies with no common comparator. The comparison looks
tempting because it seems to use the arms you care about, but it silently assumes the two trials had the
same baseline risk, which they almost never do; @prp-unanchored-bias makes the error precise and
@exm-anchored-vs-unanchored shows it as a number. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Section @sec-bucher-cancellation shows that the unanchored comparison carries a bias equal to the
difference of the two study baselines, a bias that the anchored comparison removes by construction. The
distinction between anchored and unanchored comparison organizes the whole of population-adjusted
indirect comparison: anchored methods (Chapters 17 to 20) repair residual bias in @eq-bucher-estimator,
while unanchored methods (Chapter 26) confront the baseline bias of @eq-bucher-naive head on.

## Bucher's theorem: unbiasedness {#sec-bucher-unbiased}

The next two results look almost the same, and it helps to say up front how they differ. First we prove
the *deterministic* identity: if the trials reported the true contrasts *with no sampling error at all*,
the subtraction lands exactly on the target (@prp-bucher-identity). Then we reintroduce sampling error and
show that the subtraction is still right *on average* (@thm-bucher-unbiased). The first is arithmetic; the
second is arithmetic plus one line of expectation.

::: {#prp-bucher-identity}
## Bucher's identity (exact estimates)
If $\hat d_{AC}=d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}=d_{BC}$ hold exactly and transitivity (@def-transitivity) holds,
then $\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=d_{AB}$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substitute the exact values into the estimator @eq-bucher-estimator and apply the consistency equation
@eq-bucher-consistency of @prp-transitivity-consistency:
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}=d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}. \qquad\square
$$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/Bucher.v`, `Theorem bucher_identity`]

The stochastic version replaces exact equality by unbiasedness and the substitution by linearity of
expectation. This is the theorem of @bucher1997.

::: {#thm-bucher-unbiased}
## Bucher's theorem (unbiasedness)
Suppose two studies provide estimators of pairwise relative effects of the form
$$
\hat d_{AC}=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}+\varepsilon_{AC},\qquad
\hat d_{BC}=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}+\varepsilon_{BC},
$$
with mean-zero errors $\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{AC}]=\mathbb E[\varepsilon_{BC}]=0$, so that $\hat d_{AC}$ and
$\hat d_{BC}$ are unbiased for the relative effects in their own trial populations (@prp-trial-unbiased).
Assume transitivity (@def-transitivity). Then the Bucher estimator @eq-bucher-estimator is unbiased for
the network contrast $d_{AB}$:
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]=d_{AB}.
$$
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/Bucher.v`, `Theorem bucher_unbiased`]

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This is the license for the whole method: *provided transitivity holds*, the
one-line subtraction $\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$ targets the right quantity, so an indirect estimate is a
legitimate answer to the $A$-versus-$B$ question. The theorem localizes all the risk in a single
assumption, which the remainder of the chapter, and much of the book, learns to inspect. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.proof}
Linearity of expectation applied to @eq-bucher-estimator gives
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]
=\mathbb E[\hat d_{AC}]-\mathbb E[\hat d_{BC}].
$$
By the unbiasedness hypothesis the two expectations equal the trial-population relative effects,
$$
\mathbb E[\hat d_{AC}]=d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})},\qquad
\mathbb E[\hat d_{BC}]=d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}.
$$
Transitivity (@def-transitivity) identifies each trial-population effect with the corresponding network
contrast, $d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=d_{AC}$ and $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=d_{BC}$, so
$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right]=d_{AC}-d_{BC}.
$$
Finally the consistency equation @eq-bucher-consistency, which @prp-transitivity-consistency derives from
transitivity, gives $d_{AC}-d_{BC}=d_{AB}$. Chaining the three displays yields
$\mathbb E[\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}]=d_{AB}$. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Where each hypothesis is spent.** The proof uses each assumption exactly once and at a distinct step.
Unbiasedness of the trial estimators converts expectations into trial-population effects; this is a
property of randomization within each trial and uses no cross-trial information. Transitivity converts
trial-population effects into network contrasts; this is the only cross-population assumption and is the
one that can fail. The consistency equation converts the difference of network contrasts into the target;
this is pure algebra (@lem-relative-effect-algebra) and never fails. The theorem is therefore as strong
as its weakest hypothesis, and the weakest is invariably transitivity. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The estimator is trivial; the assumption is not.** Equation @eq-bucher-estimator is one subtraction,
and one might wonder why it warrants a theorem. The answer is that the subtraction is licensed only on
the consistency-constrained set where @eq-bucher-consistency holds, and membership in that set is the
substantive scientific claim. Every population-adjusted method in Parts IV and V is, in the end, a device
for making @eq-bucher-consistency hold after a correction, or for quantifying the error when it does not.
The simplicity of Bucher's formula is exactly why the assumption that underwrites it must be stated with
care. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The Bucher variance {#sec-bucher-variance}

We already know from @thm-bucher-unbiased that the indirect estimate is centered correctly. The question
now is how *precise* it is, and the headline is simple: an indirect estimate is built from two uncertain
inputs, so its uncertainty is larger than either. The estimator @eq-bucher-estimator is a linear
combination of two trial summaries, so its variance is a two-line consequence of the bilinearity of
covariance. We first record the general identity, valid whether or not the trials are independent, because
the general form is what later chapters need when a multi-arm trial makes the two contrasts dependent.

::: {#lem-var-difference}
## Variance of a difference
For any two square-integrable random variables $U,V$ (that is, random variables with finite variance),
$$
\mathrm{Var}(U-V)=\mathrm{Var}(U)+\mathrm{Var}(V)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(U,V).
$$ {#eq-bucher-varidentity}
:::

::: {.proof}
Write $\mathrm{Var}(U-V)=\mathbb E\big[(U-V-\mathbb E[U-V])^2\big]$ and put $\tilde U=U-\mathbb E[U]$,
$\tilde V=V-\mathbb E[V]$, so $U-V-\mathbb E[U-V]=\tilde U-\tilde V$. Expanding the square and using
linearity of expectation,
$$
\mathbb E\big[(\tilde U-\tilde V)^2\big]
=\mathbb E[\tilde U^2]-2\,\mathbb E[\tilde U\tilde V]+\mathbb E[\tilde V^2]
=\mathrm{Var}(U)-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(U,V)+\mathrm{Var}(V),
$$
which is @eq-bucher-varidentity. The covariance is a symmetric bilinear form on centered variables, the
same form whose positive semidefiniteness is recorded in @thm-cov-psd. $\square$
:::

::: {#thm-bucher-variance}
## The Bucher variance
Let $\hat d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ have variances $v_{AC}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{AC})$ and
$v_{BC}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{BC})$. If the two estimators are uncorrelated, $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})=0$
(as holds when they come from disjoint sets of trials), then the Bucher estimator @eq-bucher-estimator has
variance
$$
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=v_{AC}+v_{BC}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-varsum}
In general, without the independence assumption,
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}})=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})$.
:::

[machine-checked: `theories/Bucher.v`, `Theorem bucher_variance`]

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters, and a picture.** Indirect evidence is real evidence, but it is more expensive: its
uncertainty is the *sum* of the two direct uncertainties. Independent uncertainties add in quadrature,
exactly as independent errors combine by the Pythagorean rule, so the indirect standard error is the
hypotenuse $\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}$ of the two direct standard errors. A practical
consequence, made concrete in @sec-bucher-example: an indirect comparison anchored on a *tiny*
$B$-versus-$C$ trial can be uninformative even when both direct trials are individually significant,
because the small trial's large variance is added in. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.proof}
Apply @lem-var-difference with $U=\hat d_{AC}$ and $V=\hat d_{BC}$:
$$
\mathrm{Var}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)
=v_{AC}+v_{BC}-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC}),
$$
which is the general formula. Under the independence hypothesis the covariance term is zero, leaving
$v_{AC}+v_{BC}$, equation @eq-bucher-varsum. $\square$
:::

The independence hypothesis holds in the canonical Bucher setting, where the $A$-versus-$C$ evidence and
the $B$-versus-$C$ evidence come from separate trials. It fails when a single multi-arm trial contributes
to both contrasts through a shared comparator arm: then the shared arm's sampling error enters both
$\hat d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ with the same sign, inducing a positive covariance. Intuitively, the
shared comparator's error is *partly subtracted away* rather than counted twice, so a positive covariance
*reduces* the Bucher variance below the sum @eq-bucher-varsum. The standard homoskedastic random-effects
model (a model in which every contrast is given the same variance) makes that correlation exactly one
half; the intuition is that two contrasts sharing one of their two arms overlap in half of their sampling
error, and we compute it exactly in @thm-re-nma-correlation. Because the covariance is positive, treating
correlated contrasts as independent overstates the variance, which is conservative for this comparison.

::: {#cor-bucher-efficiency}
## The price of indirectness
Under the independence hypothesis of @thm-bucher-variance, the standard error of the Bucher estimate
strictly exceeds the standard error of either direct contrast it is built from:
$$
\mathrm{SE}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=\sqrt{v_{AC}+v_{BC}}
\;>\;\max\!\left(\sqrt{v_{AC}},\,\sqrt{v_{BC}}\right),
$$
whenever both $v_{AC}>0$ and $v_{BC}>0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Since $v_{AC},v_{BC}>0$, we have $v_{AC}+v_{BC}>v_{AC}$ and $v_{AC}+v_{BC}>v_{BC}$; taking square roots,
which is monotone on the nonnegative reals, gives $\sqrt{v_{AC}+v_{BC}}>\sqrt{v_{AC}}$ and
$>\sqrt{v_{BC}}$, hence the inequality with the maximum. $\square$
:::

The corollary quantifies a fact of evidence synthesis: an indirect comparison is less precise than either
of the direct comparisons it rests on, because it accumulates the uncertainty of both. Indirect evidence
is genuine evidence, but it is statistically more expensive than a head-to-head trial of the same size.
This is one half of the case for direct trials; the other half, that indirect evidence can be *biased*
when transitivity fails, is the subject of @sec-bucher-failure.

## The common comparator cancels baseline differences {#sec-bucher-cancellation}

We now make precise the sense in which the anchor $C$ protects the comparison. Decompose each arm's
link-scale position into a study-specific baseline and a treatment-specific effect. Under transitivity the
treatment effects are population-free; the baselines are not, and they are exactly what the anchoring
removes.

::: {#def-additive-arm-decomposition}
## The additive arm decomposition
Write the marginal link-scale position of arm $k$ in study $j$ as
$$
\eta_{k(\mathcal P_j)} \;=\; \mu_j+\alpha_k,
$$ {#eq-bucher-decomp}
where $\mu_j$ is a study-specific **baseline** and $\alpha_k$ is a treatment-specific **shift** shared
across studies, with the reference treatment normalized to $\alpha_{\mathrm{ref}}=0$. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Reader translation, with a picture.** The decomposition splits each arm's position into "where the study
starts" plus "how far the treatment moves it." Concretely, normalizing the comparator as reference,
$\alpha_C=0$, so $\mu_j=\eta_{C(\mathcal P_j)}$ is literally the placebo arm's link-scale outcome in study
$j$:

```
   position eta_k(P_j)  =  mu_j (study baseline)  +  alpha_k (treatment shift)

   study AC:   arm C:  mu_AC + 0            study BC:   arm C:  mu_BC + 0
               arm A:  mu_AC + alpha_A                  arm B:  mu_BC + alpha_B

   mu_AC, mu_BC differ across studies      (different baseline risk)
   alpha_A, alpha_B, alpha_C are SHARED     (constancy of relative effects)
```

Read $\mu_j$ as "how risky study $j$'s population is under the reference treatment," its baseline log-odds
of the event; read $\alpha_k$ as "how much treatment $k$ moves that risk on the link scale," the same move
in every study. This $\mu_j$ is exactly the study-$j$ baseline (intercept) of [Notation](/notation.qmd);
the reuse of the symbol is deliberate, not a clash. Because both trials share $C$, the two baselines
$\mu_{AC}$ and $\mu_{BC}$ are the *same kind of quantity*, the placebo log-odds, measured in two different
populations, and they will differ. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The decomposition encodes constancy.** The decomposition @eq-bucher-decomp is precisely the
fixed-effect network model in the reference-treatment parameterization (@def-reference-treatment-param).
The same $\alpha_k$ appears in every study, so the contrast $\alpha_k-\alpha_{k'}$ is the population-free
network effect $d_{k'k}$: under @eq-bucher-decomp,
$d_{ab(\mathcal P_j)}=\eta_{b(\mathcal P_j)}-\eta_{a(\mathcal P_j)}=\alpha_b-\alpha_a$, free of $\mu_j$.
This is the model form of transitivity, and it is the bridge to the network meta-analysis of Chapter 15,
where the same $\mu_j$-plus-$\alpha_k$ structure is fitted to a whole network at once. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-baseline-cancellation}
## Anchoring removes both the baselines and the comparator
Assume the additive decomposition @eq-bucher-decomp with a common comparator $C$ present in both studies.
Then the Bucher estimand is free of the study baselines $\mu_{AC},\mu_{BC}$ and of the comparator effect
$\alpha_C$:
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)-(\alpha_C-\alpha_B)=\alpha_B-\alpha_A=d_{AB}.
$$
Each direct contrast already cancels its own study baseline, and the difference of contrasts then cancels
the shared comparator effect $\alpha_C$.
:::

::: {.proof}
In study $AC$ the two arms have positions $\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A$ and
$\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_C$ by @eq-bucher-decomp. Their contrast is
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\eta_{C(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=(\mu_{AC}+\alpha_C)-(\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A)=\alpha_C-\alpha_A,
$$
the baseline $\mu_{AC}$ cancelling because it is common to both arms of the same study. This is the
within-study cancellation effected by randomization. Identically, study $BC$ gives
$d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\alpha_C-\alpha_B$. Subtracting,
$$
d_{AC(\mathcal P_{AC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\alpha_C-\alpha_A)-(\alpha_C-\alpha_B)=\alpha_B-\alpha_A,
$$
the comparator effect $\alpha_C$ cancelling because it is common to both contrasts. The result
$\alpha_B-\alpha_A$ equals $d_{AB}$ by @eq-bucher-decomp. $\square$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why this matters.** This is the precise sense in which the anchor earns its keep. Differencing *within*
each trial before differencing *across* trials deletes the study baselines $\mu_j$ in two stages, so the
anchored comparison is immune to the baseline-risk differences that sink the naive comparison. It does
not, however, protect against differences in the *treatment shifts* $\alpha_k$ across populations; that is
the province of transitivity, and its failure is @sec-bucher-failure. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

The contrast with the unanchored comparison is now sharp. The naive estimator @eq-bucher-naive forgoes
the within-study cancellation and inherits the difference of baselines as outright bias.

::: {#prp-unanchored-bias}
## The unanchored comparison is biased by the baseline difference
Under the additive decomposition @eq-bucher-decomp, the unanchored estimand @eq-bucher-naive is
$$
\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})+(\alpha_A-\alpha_B)=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})-d_{AB},
$$
so, taking $\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{naive}}$ as an estimate of $-d_{AB}$ (the $A$-versus-$B$ contrast in the
reversed orientation), its bias is the difference of study baselines:
$$
\text{bias}\;=\;\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-unanchored}
The bias vanishes only in the special case $\mu_{AC}=\mu_{BC}$, that is, only when the two studies happen
to share the same baseline link-scale outcome.
:::

::: {.proof}
By @eq-bucher-decomp, $\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}=\mu_{AC}+\alpha_A$ and
$\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=\mu_{BC}+\alpha_B$. Subtracting,
$$
\eta_{A(\mathcal P_{AC})}-\eta_{B(\mathcal P_{BC})}=(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})+(\alpha_A-\alpha_B).
$$
By @eq-bucher-decomp again, $\alpha_A-\alpha_B=-(\alpha_B-\alpha_A)=-d_{AB}$. Hence the estimand equals
$(\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC})-d_{AB}$, an estimate of $-d_{AB}$ offset by $\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}$, which is the claimed
bias. It is zero precisely when $\mu_{AC}=\mu_{BC}$. $\square$
:::

::: {#exm-anchored-vs-unanchored}
## Anchored versus unanchored, on the same data
Use the two trials of the running example (computed in full in @sec-bucher-example). The placebo (arm
$C$) log-odds were $\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}=\log 0.5=-0.693$ in trial $AC$ and $\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}=\log 0.375=-0.981$
in trial $BC$; normalizing $\alpha_C=0$ makes these the two baselines,
$$
\mu_{AC}=-0.693,\qquad \mu_{BC}=-0.981,\qquad \mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}=0.288.
$$
The two statin arms happened to have *identical* event rates, $\hat\eta_A=\hat\eta_B=\log 0.25=-1.386$, so
the two analyses disagree sharply:

| Quantity | Anchored (Bucher) | Unanchored (naive) |
|---|---|---|
| what is contrasted | within-study contrasts $\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC}$ | active arms $\hat\eta_A,\hat\eta_B$ across studies |
| uses the placebo arms? | yes, as the anchor | no, they are discarded |
| estimate on the log scale | $\hat d_{AB}=0.288$ | $\hat\eta_A-\hat\eta_B=0$ |
| target it estimates | $d_{AB}$ | $-d_{AB}$ |
| odds ratio reported | $e^{0.288}=\tfrac43=1.33$ | $e^{0}=1.00$ |
| bias | none (under transitivity) | $\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}=0.288$ |

The naive comparison concludes the two statins are identical ($\mathrm{OR}=1$), because their event rates
look the same. But they are *not* comparable: statin $B$ was tested against a placebo population with a
lower event rate ($27\%$ versus $33\%$), so $B$ merely had an easier comparator. The anchored comparison
corrects for this and finds $B$ carries $\tfrac43$ the event odds of $A$. The entire discrepancy, $0.288$,
is precisely the gap between the two placebo baselines, exactly as @eq-bucher-unanchored predicts.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Why anchoring matters.** The baseline $\mu_j$ absorbs everything about study $j$'s population that
shifts the absolute outcome level: disease severity, follow-up duration, the prevalence of prognostic
variables (@def-prognostic-variable). Two trials of different drugs are run in different places at
different times and essentially never share a baseline, so $\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}$ is essentially never zero,
and the unanchored estimator @eq-bucher-naive is essentially always biased, as @exm-anchored-vs-unanchored
just showed. The anchored estimator @eq-bucher-estimator removes this bias for free, by differencing
within each study before differencing across studies. This is the whole reason anchored indirect
comparison is the default and unanchored comparison a last resort reserved for disconnected networks
(Chapter 26), where it must be propped up by strong additional assumptions to control @eq-bucher-unanchored.
Crucially, anchoring does *not* protect against differences in the *treatment effects* $\alpha_k$ across
populations; that is the province of transitivity, and its failure is @sec-bucher-failure. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## The variance of an empirical log-odds {#sec-bucher-logodds}

To turn the worked example into honest numbers we need the standard error of a single trial's log
odds-ratio. It follows from the delta method (@thm-delta-method), and it is the standard error every
applied Bucher computation uses.

::: {.remark}
**You may skip the proof on a first reading.** The only thing the worked example needs from this section
is the boxed formula @eq-bucher-logoddsvar: the estimated variance of a log odds-ratio is the sum of the
reciprocals of the four cell counts of its two-by-two table. A reader in a hurry can take this on faith
and go straight to @sec-bucher-example; the delta-method derivation below merely justifies it, repeating
the machinery of Chapter 5 (@thm-delta-method). $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#prp-logodds-variance}
## Large-sample variance of an empirical log-odds and log odds-ratio
Let an arm enroll $n$ patients of whom $r$ experience the event, with $r\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ and
$0<p<1$. Let $\hat p=r/n$ and let the empirical log-odds be $\hat\eta=\operatorname{logit}(\hat p)=\log\frac{\hat p}{1-\hat p}$.
Then, to first order,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\hat\eta)\approx\frac{1}{np(1-p)},\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\eta)=\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{n-r}.
$$ {#eq-bucher-logoddsvar}
Consequently the empirical log odds-ratio contrasting two independent arms, with event counts $r_1,r_2$
out of $n_1,n_2$, has estimated variance $\big(\tfrac1{r_1}+\tfrac1{n_1-r_1}\big)+\big(\tfrac1{r_2}+\tfrac1{n_2-r_2}\big)$,
the sum of the inverse cell counts of the underlying two-by-two table.
:::

::: {.proof}
The logit $g(p)=\log p-\log(1-p)$ has derivative $g'(p)=\frac1p+\frac1{1-p}=\frac{1}{p(1-p)}$. Since
$\hat p$ is the mean of $n$ independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables, $\mathbb E[\hat p]=p$ and
$\mathrm{Var}(\hat p)=p(1-p)/n$, and by the central limit theorem $\sqrt n(\hat p-p)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N(0,p(1-p))$.
The delta method (@thm-delta-method) applied to $g$ gives
$$
\sqrt n\big(g(\hat p)-g(p)\big)\xrightarrow{d}\mathcal N\!\big(0,\,[g'(p)]^2\,p(1-p)\big),
\qquad [g'(p)]^2\,p(1-p)=\frac{p(1-p)}{p^2(1-p)^2}=\frac{1}{p(1-p)},
$$
so $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\eta)\approx\frac{1}{np(1-p)}$. Substituting the plug-in estimate $\hat p=r/n$,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\eta)=\frac{1}{n\hat p(1-\hat p)}=\frac{1}{n\cdot\frac{r}{n}\cdot\frac{n-r}{n}}
=\frac{n}{r(n-r)}=\frac{(n-r)+r}{r(n-r)}=\frac1r+\frac1{n-r},
$$
which is @eq-bucher-logoddsvar. The two arms are independent, so by @lem-var-difference (with zero
covariance) the variance of their difference of log-odds is the sum of the two arm variances; collecting
the four reciprocals gives the stated table formula. The normal approximation underlying a Wald interval
is justified by the asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator (@thm-mle-asymptotic-normality),
of which $\hat\eta$ is an instance. $\square$
:::

## A worked Bucher comparison on the log odds-ratio scale {#sec-bucher-example}

We carry a complete example from raw counts to a confidence interval, so that every number can be checked
by hand. The event is an unfavorable outcome (a cardiovascular event); larger log-odds means worse.

::: {.remark}
**Recipe: Bucher from published trials.** Most of the time you will not have raw counts but a reported
estimate and interval. The five-step recipe is then:

1. **Recover each standard error** from a reported $95\%$ interval on the log scale:
   $\mathrm{SE}=(\text{upper}-\text{lower})/(2\times 1.96)$, both endpoints on the log scale.
2. **Line up the orientation**: express both direct effects as "versus the common comparator $C$" on the
   same log scale (log OR, log RR, or log HR), so that $\hat d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ mean $\eta_C-\eta_A$
   and $\eta_C-\eta_B$.
3. **Subtract**: $\hat d_{AB}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}$.
4. **Add variances** (if the trials are independent):
   $\mathrm{SE}(\hat d_{AB})=\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}_{AC}^2+\mathrm{SE}_{BC}^2}$.
5. **Interval, then back-transform**: form a Wald interval on the log scale, then exponentiate the
   estimate and both interval endpoints to report a ratio.

The example below runs this recipe starting one step earlier, from the raw tables. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {#exm-bucher-logor}
## Indirect comparison of $A$ and $B$ through a common comparator $C$

**Orientation check.** We report on the chapter's $d_{ab}=\eta_b-\eta_a$ scale. The event is unfavorable,
so a *positive* contrast flags *higher, worse* odds. We expect both statins to beat placebo, so we expect
$\hat d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A>0$ and $\hat d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B>0$ (placebo worse than each statin), and the
target is $d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A$, "$B$ versus $A$, higher is worse."

Two randomized trials report the following two-by-two tables.

Study $AC$ (treatment $A$ versus comparator $C$):

| Arm | Events $r$ | Non-events $n-r$ | Total $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $A$ | $30$ | $120$ | $150$ |
| $C$ | $50$ | $100$ | $150$ |

Study $BC$ (treatment $B$ versus comparator $C$):

| Arm | Events $r$ | Non-events $n-r$ | Total $n$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $B$ | $40$ | $160$ | $200$ |
| $C$ | $60$ | $160$ | $220$ |

**Step 1: arm log-odds.** With $\hat\eta=\log\frac{r}{n-r}$,
$$
\hat\eta_A=\log\tfrac{30}{120}=\log 0.25=-1.38629,\qquad
\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}=\log\tfrac{50}{100}=\log 0.5=-0.69315,
$$
$$
\hat\eta_B=\log\tfrac{40}{160}=\log 0.25=-1.38629,\qquad
\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}=\log\tfrac{60}{160}=\log 0.375=-0.98083.
$$

**Step 2: direct contrasts.** Using the [Notation](/notation.qmd) order $d_{kC}=\eta_C-\eta_k$,
$$
\hat d_{AC}=\hat\eta_C^{(AC)}-\hat\eta_A=-0.69315-(-1.38629)=0.69315=\log 2,
$$
$$
\hat d_{BC}=\hat\eta_C^{(BC)}-\hat\eta_B=-0.98083-(-1.38629)=0.40546=\log 1.5.
$$
Both are positive, as the orientation check anticipated. On the odds-ratio scale the comparator $C$ has
twice the event odds of $A$ and one and a half times the event odds of $B$; equivalently $A$ and $B$ are
both protective relative to $C$, with $A$ the more so.

**Step 3: direct variances** by @prp-logodds-variance, summing inverse cell counts,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat d_{AC})=\tfrac1{30}+\tfrac1{120}+\tfrac1{50}+\tfrac1{100}=0.071667,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.26771,
$$
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat d_{BC})=\tfrac1{40}+\tfrac1{160}+\tfrac1{60}+\tfrac1{160}=0.054167,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.23274.
$$

**Step 4: the Bucher estimate.** By @eq-bucher-estimator and @eq-bucher-varsum,
$$
\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}=\hat d_{AC}-\hat d_{BC}=0.69315-0.40546=0.28768=\log\tfrac43,
$$
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}\!\left(\hat d_{AB}^{\,\mathrm{Bucher}}\right)=0.071667+0.054167=0.125833,\qquad
\mathrm{SE}=0.35473.
$$

**Step 5: interval and back-transformation.** A $95\%$ Wald interval on the log scale is
$0.28768\pm 1.95996\times 0.35473=0.28768\pm 0.69526=(-0.40758,\,0.98293)$. Exponentiating, the indirect
odds ratio of the event comparing $B$ to $A$ is
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{AB}=e^{0.28768}=1.3333=\tfrac43,\qquad
95\%\ \mathrm{CI}=(e^{-0.40758},\,e^{0.98293})=(0.665,\,2.672).
$$
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**Final interpretation, in both orientations.** On this chapter's $d_{AB}=\eta_B-\eta_A$ scale, the event
odds for statin $B$ are estimated as $1.33$ times those for statin $A$; equivalently, the event odds for
$A$ are $1/1.33=0.75$ times those for $B$. Either way, the point estimate favors $A$ as the better statin.
But the $95\%$ interval for the odds ratio, $(0.67,\,2.67)$, comfortably includes $1$, so on this evidence
the difference is not statistically distinguishable from no difference. And the estimate is trustworthy
*only under transitivity*: it assumes the two trials' populations shared the distribution of any covariate
that modifies the statin effect on the log odds-ratio scale. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Three further features of the example repay attention.

::: {.remark}
**Ratios divide; logs subtract.** The indirect odds ratio $\tfrac43$ is exactly the ratio of the two
reported odds ratios, $2/1.5=\tfrac43$, which is the multiplicative face of the additive identity
$\log\tfrac43=\log 2-\log 1.5$. Had we (wrongly) subtracted the odds ratios, $2-1.5=0.5$, we would have
produced a number with no meaning. The additive scale of @lem-relative-effect-algebra is not optional
bookkeeping; it is where the cancellation lives. The same arithmetic works verbatim on any additive
scale: if a rheumatoid-arthritis network instead reported $\hat d_{AC}=-0.40$ and $\hat d_{BC}=-0.15$ as
log *hazard* ratios of disease progression, then $\hat d_{AB}=-0.40-(-0.15)=-0.25$, a hazard ratio
$e^{-0.25}=0.78$; only the name of the scale changed. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**The price of indirectness, concretely.** The Bucher standard error $0.355$ exceeds both direct standard
errors $0.268$ and $0.233$, as @cor-bucher-efficiency guarantees. The effect on inference is stark. The
direct $A$-versus-$C$ contrast is significant ($z=0.69315/0.26771=2.59$), the direct $B$-versus-$C$
contrast borderline ($z=0.40546/0.23274=1.74$), yet the indirect $A$-versus-$B$ contrast is firmly
inconclusive ($z=0.28768/0.35473=0.81$, two-sided $p\approx 0.42$), its $95\%$ interval for the odds
ratio running from $0.67$ to $2.67$ and comfortably including $1$. Two informative direct comparisons can
combine into an uninformative indirect one. $\blacktriangleleft$
:::

::: {.remark}
**What the number means, and what it assumes.** The estimate $\widehat{\mathrm{OR}}_{AB}=\tfrac43$ is
unbiased for the true $A$-versus-$B$ odds ratio *only under transitivity*: the populations of the two
trials must share the distribution of any covariate that modifies the treatment effect on the log
odds-ratio scale. If, for instance, study $BC$ enrolled younger patients and age modifies the effect of
$B$, then $\hat d_{BC}$ estimates the effect in a younger population than the one in which $\hat d_{AC}$
estimates the effect of $A$, and the subtraction mixes populations. No amount of data fixes this; it is a
bias, not a variance, and it is invisible in the standard error $0.355$. Diagnosing and repairing it is
the subject of node-splitting (@def-node-splitting), a diagnostic that splits a comparison into its direct
and indirect parts and checks whether they agree, and of population adjustment (Parts IV and V).
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

## When transitivity fails {#sec-bucher-failure}

Bucher's theorem is exact under its hypotheses, so every difficulty with indirect comparison is a
difficulty with a hypothesis. The variance hypothesis (independence) is mild and is relaxed by an honest
covariance term, @thm-bucher-variance. The unbiasedness hypothesis (randomization) holds by design in the
trials that anchored comparisons are built from. The hypothesis that bears the weight is transitivity,
and it fails for a definite mechanism: an **effect modifier** (@def-effect-modifier) whose distribution
differs between the trial populations.

To see the mechanism, suppose a binary covariate $Z$ modifies the $B$-versus-$C$ effect, so that the
conditional contrast $d_{BC}(z)$ takes one value at $z=0$ and another at $z=1$. The marginal effect
@eq-bucher-reldef is then a weighted average of $d_{BC}(0)$ and $d_{BC}(1)$ with weights given by the
prevalence of $Z$ in the population. If study $BC$ has a different prevalence of $Z$ than the population
in which we wish to report $A$ versus $B$, the marginal $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ differs from
$d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}$, transitivity @eq-bucher-transitivity is violated, the consistency equation
@eq-bucher-consistency no longer holds, and the Bucher estimator @eq-bucher-estimator is biased by exactly
the discrepancy $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}$.

::: {#exm-transitivity-failure}
## A transitivity failure as a specific number
Let $Z$ be presence of diabetes, an effect modifier of the statin-$B$ effect. On the log odds-ratio scale,
the conditional $B$-versus-$C$ contrast is $d_{BC}(Z=0)=0.4$ in non-diabetics and $d_{BC}(Z=1)=1.0$ in
diabetics (statin $B$ is more protective in diabetics). Diabetes is more common in the $BC$ trial than in
the target population where we want the answer:

| $Z$ (diabetes) | conditional $d_{BC}(Z)$ | prevalence in $BC$ trial | prevalence in target $\mathcal P_{AB}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $Z=0$ | $0.4$ | $0.4$ | $0.8$ |
| $Z=1$ | $1.0$ | $0.6$ | $0.2$ |

The marginal $B$-versus-$C$ effects are the prevalence-weighted averages
$$
\begin{aligned}
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})} &= 0.4\times 0.4 + 1.0\times 0.6 = 0.76,\\
d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})} &= 0.4\times 0.8 + 1.0\times 0.2 = 0.52.
\end{aligned}
$$
Suppose the $A$-versus-$C$ effect is unaffected by $Z$ and equals $d_{AC}=0.6$ in every population. The
*true* target contrast is $d_{AB}=d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}=0.6-0.52=0.08$. The Bucher estimand,
however, subtracts the $BC$ trial's own marginal effect,
$d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}=0.6-0.76=-0.16$. The bias is
$$
-0.16-0.08=-0.24=-\big(d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}\big),
$$
a log-odds-ratio error of $-0.24$, a multiplicative error of $e^{-0.24}\approx 0.79$ in the odds ratio,
about $21\%$. It does not shrink as the trials grow: it is a bias, not a variance, and it is invisible in
any standard error. This is the mechanism the rest of the book is built to detect and repair.
$\blacktriangleleft$
:::

Chapter 16 makes this calculation general and names the resulting failure (@thm-failure-of-bucher), and
shows how it compounds with the non-collapsibility of the odds ratio and with **ecological bias**
(@def-ecological-bias), the bias that arises when a relationship estimated at the trial-average level does
not hold at the individual level. The point to carry forward is structural: prognostic variables that are
not effect modifiers do *not* break transitivity, because they shift the baselines $\mu_j$, which
@prp-baseline-cancellation already cancels; only effect modifiers, which alter the $\alpha_k$ across
populations, can break it.

When both direct and indirect evidence exist for the same contrast, the consistency equation becomes
testable by comparing them: this is **node-splitting** (@def-node-splitting, @thm-consistency-closure),
the diagnostic developed in Chapter 15 that splits a comparison into its direct and indirect parts and
checks whether they agree. A significant discrepancy is the empirical signature of a transitivity failure
and the trigger for the population-adjustment methods that occupy the remainder of the book.

Transitivity is also the assumption that connects this chapter to the transportability framework of
Chapter 12. Transportability asks when a relative effect measured in one population may be carried to
another; transitivity is exactly the special case, direct transportability (@def-transportability,
@thm-direct-transportability), in which the relative effect is assumed to transport *unchanged* from each
trial population to the target. In the language of @exm-transitivity-failure, transportability would have
us reweight the conditional contrasts $d_{BC}(z)$ to the target prevalence of $Z$ before subtracting; the
population-adjustment methods of Parts IV and V are precisely the machinery that performs that reweighting
when it is needed. Transitivity is the assumption that it is *not* needed, and the bridge to Chapter 12 is
the tool for the cases where it is.

## Notes and references {#sec-bucher-notes}

The anchored indirect comparison and the estimator @eq-bucher-estimator are due to @bucher1997, who
introduced the difference of log relative effects and its variance @eq-bucher-varsum as the basis for
indirect comparison in meta-analysis of randomized trials. The framing in terms of constancy of relative
effects and transitivity, and the embedding of the estimator in the network model with the
reference-treatment decomposition @eq-bucher-decomp, follows @dias2018nma and the thesis of
@phillippo2019thesis (Eq. 1.2 for constancy, Eq. 1.3 for the indirect estimator). The two-layer
cancellation argument of @sec-bucher-cancellation, separating the within-study cancellation of baselines
from the across-study cancellation of the comparator, is the algebraic core of why anchored comparisons
are preferred to unanchored ones; the bias formula @eq-bucher-unanchored for the naive comparison is the
quantity that unanchored population adjustment (Chapter 26) must control. The delta-method variance of the
empirical log-odds (@prp-logodds-variance) is classical; the sum-of-inverse-cell-counts form is the
standard error reported by every two-by-two table routine.

This chapter corresponds to results D.1 (transitivity), D.2 (Bucher's theorem), D.3 (the Bucher variance),
and D.4 (constancy of relative effects) of the proof catalogue in
`proofs/D_network_meta_analysis.md`. The network-level material that builds on Bucher's identity, namely
the parameterizations (@def-baseline-shift-param, @def-reference-treatment-param), identifiability via the
graph incidence rank (@thm-fe-nma-identifiability), the random-effects contrast correlation
(@thm-re-nma-correlation), the consistency closure and node-splitting (@thm-consistency-closure,
@def-node-splitting), and goodness-of-fit (@def-residual-deviance, @def-dic), is developed in Chapter 15;
the breakdown of transitivity under effect modification (@thm-failure-of-bucher, @def-ecological-bias) is
developed in Chapter 16. When the two direct contrasts are themselves pooled over several trials, the
pooling is the pairwise meta-analysis of Chapter 13 (@thm-fixed-effect-blue for the fixed-effect
inverse-variance estimate, @thm-dersimonian-laird for the random-effects estimate), and Bucher's identity
operates on the pooled summaries. The connection to transportability (@def-transportability,
@thm-direct-transportability) is developed in Chapter 12.

Three results of this chapter have machine-checked counterparts in the companion Coq development, in
`theories/Bucher.v`. The exact identity @prp-bucher-identity is `Theorem bucher_identity`; the
unbiasedness theorem @thm-bucher-unbiased is `Theorem bucher_unbiased`; the variance theorem
@thm-bucher-variance is `Theorem bucher_variance`. The transitivity definition @def-transitivity and the
equivalence @prp-transitivity-consistency are formalized as `Definition transitivity` together with
`Lemma transitivity_subtract` and `Lemma subtract_transitivity`. The Coq development treats expectation,
variance, and covariance as abstract operators satisfying linearity and the difference identity
@eq-bucher-varidentity, exactly the structure used in the proofs above, so that the formalization captures
the algebraic content of Bucher's theorem while leaving the measure-theoretic construction of those
operators to the caller.

## Exercises {#sec-bucher-exercises}

The exercises progress from warm-up to challenge, and are tagged by kind. An exercise marked $\star$ has a
full worked solution in Appendix F. The first two are gentle checks of orientation and interpretation; the
later ones build toward the network theory of Chapters 15 and 16.

::: {#exr-bucher-warmup}
**Warm-up. Identify, orient, compute.** A health technology assessment has two independent trials against
a common comparator $C$ (placebo). Trial $AC$ reports the effect of a new drug on the log odds-ratio scale
as $\hat d_{AC}=\eta_C-\eta_A=0.50$ with $\mathrm{SE}=0.20$; trial $BC$ reports
$\hat d_{BC}=\eta_C-\eta_B=0.30$ with $\mathrm{SE}=0.15$. The outcome is unfavorable, so higher odds is
worse. (a) Name the common comparator and the target contrast. (b) State whether a positive $\hat d_{AC}$
means the new drug $A$ is better or worse than $C$, and why. (c) Compute the Bucher estimate $\hat d_{AB}$
and its standard error. (d) Back-transform to an odds ratio for $B$ versus $A$ and say, in one sentence,
which drug the point estimate favors. (e) State the transitivity assumption you relied on, in one plain
sentence.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-interpret}
**Interpretation. What breaks it, and what does not.** In the setting of @exr-bucher-warmup, suppose you
learn that trial $BC$ enrolled much older patients than trial $AC$. (a) If age strongly modifies the
effect of drug $B$, is the age difference a threat to the Bucher comparison, and which assumption does it
threaten? (b) Would enrolling more patients in each trial remove the threat? Explain in one sentence why
or why not. (c) Now suppose instead that age predicts the outcome but does *not* change the size of any
treatment effect. Explain why the anchored comparison is then unharmed, naming the result
(@prp-baseline-cancellation) that does the work.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-recompute}
**Computation. A Bucher computation from summaries.** Two trials report log hazard ratios on the
proportional-hazards scale: $\hat d_{AC}=-0.51$ with $\mathrm{SE}=0.18$, and $\hat d_{BC}=-0.22$ with
$\mathrm{SE}=0.13$, the contrasts being independent. Compute the indirect log hazard ratio of $A$ versus
$B$, its standard error, a $95\%$ confidence interval, and the back-transformed hazard ratio with
interval. State the transitivity assumption you are relying on in words.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-tables}
**Computation. From raw tables.** Repeat the worked example @exm-bucher-logor with the tables: study $AC$
has $A:24/120$ and $C:48/160$; study $BC$ has $B:20/100$ and $C:30/150$. Report the two direct log
odds-ratios with standard errors, the Bucher estimate with standard error, and the indirect odds ratio
with $95\%$ interval. Verify that the indirect odds ratio equals the ratio of the two direct odds ratios.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-scales}
**Proof. Additivity holds on the right scales.** Prove that the antisymmetry and additivity laws
@lem-relative-effect-algebra hold for the log risk-ratio contrast $d_{ab}=\log\bar\mu_b-\log\bar\mu_a$ and
for the mean-difference contrast $d_{ab}=\bar\mu_b-\bar\mu_a$, and show by a numerical counterexample that
they fail for the risk-ratio contrast taken on the ratio scale itself, $\bar\mu_b/\bar\mu_a$ (that is,
that $\bar\mu_C/\bar\mu_A\ne(\bar\mu_C/\bar\mu_B)\cdot\text{(something additive)}$ unless one first takes
logarithms). Conclude that Bucher's subtraction is a statement about the link scale.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-unanchored}
**Computation. The cost of dropping the anchor.** Using the additive decomposition @eq-bucher-decomp,
suppose $\mu_{AC}=-1.2$, $\mu_{BC}=-1.8$, $\alpha_A=-0.7$, $\alpha_B=-0.4$, $\alpha_C=0$ on the logit
scale. Compute the true network contrast $d_{AB}$, the anchored estimand $d_{AC}-d_{BC}$, and the
unanchored estimand @eq-bucher-naive, and verify that the unanchored estimand is off by exactly
$\mu_{AC}-\mu_{BC}$ as @prp-unanchored-bias predicts. Comment on which of the five parameters an anchored
comparison is immune to.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-chain}
**Proof. A longer chain.** Generalize Bucher's identity to a path of comparators $A\to C\to D\to B$, in
which trial $AC$ estimates $d_{AC}$, trial $CD$ estimates $d_{CD}$, and trial $DB$ estimates $d_{DB}$, all
independent. Using @lem-relative-effect-algebra, derive the chained indirect estimator of $d_{AB}$ as a
signed sum of the three direct contrasts, prove it unbiased under transitivity along the path, and show
its variance is the sum of the three direct variances. Explain why each additional link strictly inflates
the variance.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-correlated}
**($\star$, challenge) Correlated contrasts from a three-arm trial.** Suppose a single three-arm trial
reports both $\hat d_{AC}$ and $\hat d_{BC}$ (arms $A$, $B$, $C$ in one study), so the shared comparator
arm makes the two contrasts correlated with $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat d_{AC},\hat d_{BC})=\rho\sqrt{v_{AC}v_{BC}}$
for some $\rho>0$. Using the general formula in @thm-bucher-variance, write the variance of the Bucher
estimate of $d_{AB}$ and show it is strictly smaller than $v_{AC}+v_{BC}$. For the homoskedastic structure
in which both contrasts share a comparator arm of variance $\sigma^2$ and have arm-level variance
$\sigma^2$ in each non-comparator arm, show $\rho=\tfrac12$ and recover the variance of the within-study
$A$-versus-$B$ contrast directly; reconcile your answer with @thm-re-nma-correlation.
:::

::: {#exr-bucher-transitivity-bias}
**($\star$, interpretation) Quantifying a transitivity failure.** A binary effect modifier $Z$ acts on the
$B$-versus-$C$ contrast so that the conditional log odds-ratios are $d_{BC}(Z=0)=0.2$ and $d_{BC}(Z=1)=0.8$
(on the link scale, treating these conditional contrasts as collapsible for simplicity). Study $BC$ has
$\Pr(Z=1)=0.7$, while the target population $\mathcal P_{AB}$ in which we wish to report $A$ versus $B$ has
$\Pr(Z=1)=0.3$. The $A$-versus-$C$ contrast is unaffected by $Z$ and equals $d_{AC}=0.6$ in every
population. Compute the marginal $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$ and $d_{BC(\mathcal P_{AB})}$, the true target
contrast $d_{AB}$, the Bucher estimand $d_{AC}-d_{BC(\mathcal P_{BC})}$, and hence the bias of the
unadjusted indirect comparison. Identify which quantity an effect-modifier adjustment (Chapter 17 onward)
must reweight to remove the bias, and explain why a prognostic variable that shifted only the baseline
would have created no bias at all.
:::
